new.title: Step into Belle Époque Nice at the Musée Masséna
new.desc: One of the last grand 19th century villas on the Promenade des Anglais now holds the city's history museum. Its rooms and seaside garden tell the story of Nice from the County era to the glamour of the winter season.
new.tip: The garden is free to wander even if you skip the museum, and it is a shady pause between two stretches of the Promenade.
new.q: Musée Masséna, Promenade des Anglais, Nice

new.title: Find the Musée des Beaux-Arts Jules Chéret
new.desc: The city's fine arts museum fills a 19th century villa in the quiet streets of the Baumettes district, west of the centre. It is named after Jules Chéret, the poster artist who spent his last years in Nice, and holds many of his works.
new.tip: Few visitors make it this far west, so you often have the rooms to yourself. Nice residents get in free with the municipal museum pass.
new.q: Musée des Beaux-Arts Jules Chéret, Avenue des Baumettes, Nice

new.title: Look up inside the Chapelle de la Miséricorde
new.desc: Right on the Cours Saleya, the chapel of the Black Penitents is considered the masterpiece of Niçois baroque. Behind a modest façade hides an oval interior of gilding, stucco and painted ceilings.
new.tip: It is often shut, so watch for guided visits run by the city or come for a Sunday service.
new.q: Chapelle de la Miséricorde, Cours Saleya, Nice

new.title: Walk the terraces of the Cimetière du Château
new.desc: Opened in 1783 on the site of the razed citadel, this terraced cemetery holds some 2,800 tombs with sweeping views over the port and the city. Gaston Leroux, Emil Jellinek of Mercedes fame, Alexander Herzen and Garibaldi's mother all lie here.
new.tip: Look for the pyramid at the entrance, a memorial to the 200 or so victims of the 1881 opera house fire.
new.q: Cimetière du Château, Nice

new.title: Meet the twin towers of the Basilique Notre-Dame
new.desc: Halfway along the busy Avenue Jean-Médecin, Nice's largest church rises with two square towers and a big rose window, a neo-Gothic piece of northern France dropped among the shops.
new.tip: Step in from the shopping crowds for a few minutes of quiet. Tram line 1 stops right outside.
new.q: Basilique Notre-Dame de l'Assomption, Avenue Jean Médecin, Nice

new.title: Admire the pink dome of the Hotel Negresco
new.desc: Opened in 1912 by Henri Negresco, the palace hotel with its pink and green dome is the most famous façade on the Promenade des Anglais. It is also home to the restaurant Le Chantecler.
new.tip: For a glimpse inside without staying the night, have a drink at the hotel bar.
new.q: Hôtel Negresco, 37 Promenade des Anglais, Nice

new.title: See naive art in a pink château at Fabron
new.desc: The Musée International d'Art Naïf Anatole Jakovsky, opened in 1982, shows naive painting from the 17th to the 20th century inside the pink Château Sainte-Hélène, in the western hills of Fabron.
new.tip: It closes over lunch, so plan a morning or an afternoon. Entry is cheap, and free for Nice residents.
new.q: Musée International d'Art Naïf Anatole Jakovsky, Avenue de Fabron, Nice

new.title: Discover the concrete domes of Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc
new.desc: Begun in 1914 and finished in 1933, this church north of the station looks almost futuristic: three egg shaped concrete domes, eight smaller ones and a 64 metre openwork bell tower. Inside, Eugène Klementieff painted the Stations of the Cross in the 1930s.
new.tip: It is in a residential district well off the tourist trail, an easy walk from the Libération market.
new.q: Église Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc, Nice

new.title: Shop like a local at the Libération market
new.desc: Around the old Gare du Sud and Place du Général de Gaulle, the Libération market is where Niçois do their real shopping: fruit, vegetables, local cheese and a separate fish market, every morning except Monday.
new.tip: Come before noon, as stalls pack up around 12:30. The prices are friendlier than on the Cours Saleya.
new.q: Marché de la Libération, Place du Général de Gaulle, Nice

new.title: Buy candied fruit at Maison Auer, sweet maker since 1820
new.desc: Across from the opera, this family confectioner and chocolatier has been making candied fruit since 1820. Its signature is the amande princesse, alongside fruit jellies, marrons glacés and orangettes.
new.tip: The ornate old shop is a sight in itself. A small box of candied clementines makes a classic Niçois gift.
new.q: Maison Auer, 7 Rue Saint-François de Paule, Nice

new.title: Taste Niçois olive oil at Alziari
new.desc: Behind its blue shopfront on Rue Saint-François de Paule, Alziari sells olive oil from the small Cailletier olive, the variety behind the Nice appellation, along with olives, tapenades and its famous blue and yellow tins.
new.tip: Ask to taste before you buy, and look for the AOP Huile d'olive de Nice label.
new.q: Nicolas Alziari, 14 Rue Saint-François de Paule, Nice

new.title: Get your name on the chalkboard at La Merenda
new.desc: A tiny old town bistro where Dominique Le Stanc, once a Michelin starred chef at the Negresco, cooks Niçois classics such as courgette flower fritters and pasta with pistou in a cramped kitchen.
new.tip: There is no phone booking: drop by in the morning to put your name down. Cash only, and closed at weekends.
new.q: La Merenda, 4 Rue Raoul Bosio, Nice

new.title: Start the day with a merenda at Cave de la Tour
new.desc: Run by the same family since 1947, this wine bar in the old town opens at 8am with plates of cured meats from the hills, which draw the market butchers and fishmongers. Wine by the glass comes from upturned barrels.
new.tip: Come for an early glass with the regulars, or at lunch for the short slate of dishes from the day's market.
new.q: Cave de la Tour, 3 Rue de la Tour, Nice

new.title: Have an apéro at Les Distilleries Idéales
new.desc: One of the prettiest bars in the old town, with old distillery decor, a long row of beer taps and a terrace on Rue de la Préfecture, a few steps from Place Rossetti.
new.tip: Happy hour runs from 6pm to 8pm, so arrive early for a terrace table.
new.q: Les Distilleries Idéales, 24 Rue de la Préfecture, Nice

new.title: Eat homemade pasta at the Bar des Oiseaux
new.desc: A small old town bistro on Rue Saint-Vincent with a modern touch on Niçois food and fresh pasta, from squid ravioli to seafood linguine. It has been listed in the Michelin guide in recent years.
new.tip: Book ahead, it is closed on Sundays and Mondays and fills up with locals.
new.q: Le Bar des Oiseaux, 5 Rue Saint-Vincent, Nice

new.title: Dine on the rock at Le Plongeoir
new.desc: A restaurant perched on a rock in the sea below Mont Boron, reached by a footbridge. The rock was a fishing boat base in the 19th century, and the Belle Époque made it a spot for tea and cocktails above the waves.
new.tip: It closes in winter, so check the reopening date. Book a table at sunset.
new.q: Le Plongeoir, 60 Boulevard Franck Pilatte, Nice

new.title: Catch a concert at the Nice Jazz Festival
new.desc: First held in 1948 and every year since 1971, the Nice Jazz Festival is often called the first jazz festival to gain international fame. In July, concerts fill the Théâtre de Verdure and the stage by Place Masséna.
new.tip: Buy a pass for several nights, and come early to get close to the stage.
new.q: Théâtre de Verdure, Nice

new.title: Cheer on OGC Nice at the Allianz Riviera
new.desc: The city's football club, the Gym, plays at the Allianz Riviera in the Saint-Isidore district of the Var plain, Match nights bring the whole city together in red and black.
new.tip: Take tram line 3 to the stadium and avoid driving. Tickets for big matches sell out fast.
new.q: Allianz Riviera, Nice

new.title: Walk the olive terraces of the Parc du Vinaigrier
new.desc: On the slopes of Mont Vinaigrier between Nice and Villefranche, 25 hectares of old olive terraces, Aleppo pines and holm oaks were a farm until the 1960s. Today it is a protected natural park with views over the city.
new.tip: Bring water and good shoes: the paths are steep and there is no café.
new.q: Parc du Vinaigrier, Nice

new.title: Wander the Jardin Botanique above the airport
new.desc: On the western heights of Nice, the city's botanical garden grows more than 3,500 species on about three hectares, with views over the sea, the mouth of the Var and the Estérel hills. It opened in 1991.
new.tip: Entry is free. It is high on the Corniche Fleurie, so take a bus or a car.
new.q: Jardin Botanique, Avenue de la Corniche Fleurie, Nice

new.title: See what is on at Le 109 in the old slaughterhouses
new.desc: The city's former abattoirs, built between 1957 and 1967 and closed in 1999, are now Le 109, a centre for contemporary culture on Route de Turin. Artists' studios, festivals, concerts and exhibitions fill its big sheds.
new.tip: Check the programme first: there is not always something open. The free Éclairage Public festival in June is a good way in.
new.q: Le 109, 89 Route de Turin, Nice

new.title: Explore the terraces and shows at Villa Arson
new.desc: An 18th century villa wrapped in Michel Marot's modernist art school of the early 1970s, stepping down a hill in three terraces of patios and roof gardens. Its contemporary art centre puts on temporary exhibitions.
new.tip: Check what is showing, then take time to walk the terraces and the old gardens of pines and cypresses.
new.q: Villa Arson, 20 Avenue Stephen Liégeard, Nice

new.title: See Picasso's War and Peace in Vallauris
new.desc: In 1952 Picasso painted two huge facing panels, War and Peace, on the vault of the old Romanesque chapel of the castle of Vallauris, the pottery town where he lived. It is now a national museum.
new.tip: The same castle holds the Magnelli and ceramics museum. Closed on Tuesdays.
new.q: Musée national Picasso La Guerre et la Paix, Place de la Libération, Vallauris

new.title: Spot the giant mosaic of the Musée Fernand Léger
new.desc: Below the village of Biot, a museum built for Fernand Léger holds the largest collection of his work. Its façade is covered by a huge, brightly coloured mosaic you can see from the road.
new.tip: Combine it with the glassworks nearby and a walk up to the old village.
new.q: Musée national Fernand Léger, Biot

new.title: Live like an ancient Greek at Villa Kérylos
new.desc: Archaeologist Théodore Reinach had this villa built between 1902 and 1908 on a rocky point at Beaulieu-sur-Mer, as a faithful version of a house on Delos with modern comforts. Frescoes, mosaics and inlaid furniture fill every room.
new.tip: It is a short walk from Beaulieu station, and the coastal walk to Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat starts nearby.
new.q: Villa Kérylos, Beaulieu-sur-Mer

new.title: Explore Lawrence Johnston's Serre de la Madone
new.desc: Lawrence Johnston, creator of Hidcote in England, made this garden in a valley above Menton from 1924, filling terraces with rare plants from around the world. It is a listed historic monument.
new.tip: Combine it with the village of Gorbio up the same road, and check opening days before going.
new.q: Serre de la Madone, 74 Route de Gorbio, Menton

new.title: Climb the keep of Roquebrune castle
new.desc: Built at the end of the 10th century by the Count of Ventimiglia to keep out Saracen raiders, the castle of Roquebrune later belonged to the Grimaldi for centuries. It towers over the medieval village of covered lanes.
new.tip: From the top, look down on Cap Martin and across to Monaco.
new.q: Château de Roquebrune-Cap-Martin

new.title: Wander the vaulted lanes of Peillon
new.desc: Peillon clings to a rocky spur above the Paillon valley, a short drive from Nice. Its Chapelle des Pénitents Blancs holds late 15th century frescoes by Jean Canavesio.
new.tip: Leave the car at the entrance and explore on foot: the village is a tangle of steps and covered passages.
new.q: Peillon

new.title: See the Sistine Chapel of the Alps at Notre-Dame des Fontaines
new.desc: In a quiet valley near La Brigue in the Roya, this pilgrimage chapel is covered with some 225 square metres of frescoes by Giovanni Baleison and Giovanni Canavesio, finished in 1492, including a dramatic Last Judgment.
new.tip: Visits are by appointment through the La Brigue tourist office. Children under 12 go free.
new.q: Notre-Dame des Fontaines, La Brigue

new.title: Find the rugby founder's grave above Menton
new.desc: The Cimetière du Vieux Château crowns the old town of Menton with terraced tombs, a small Russian Orthodox chapel and wide views of the coast. William Webb Ellis, credited with inventing rugby, is buried here.
new.tip: Climb up through the old town lanes in the morning, before the heat.
new.q: Cimetière du Vieux Château, Menton

new.title: Visit Renoir's last home among the olives of Cagnes
new.desc: Renoir moved to the Domaine des Collettes in Cagnes-sur-Mer in 1908 and painted here until his death in 1919. The house and his two studios stand much as he left them, in an old olive grove.
new.tip: Bring a picnic for the olive grove, and walk on to the hilltop village of Haut-de-Cagnes.
new.q: Musée Renoir, 19 Chemin des Collettes, Cagnes-sur-Mer

new.title: Eat fish on the quay at La Mère Germaine
new.desc: On the harbour of Villefranche-sur-Mer since 1938, this family restaurant is now run by the founder's grandson. It serves fresh and wild fish on a terrace right above the boats.
new.tip: Book a terrace table for lunch and walk it off around the citadel afterwards.
new.q: La Mère Germaine, 7 Quai Amiral Courbet, Villefranche-sur-Mer

new.title: Splurge at Mirazur on the Italian border
new.desc: Mauro Colagreco's restaurant in Menton holds three Michelin stars and was named the World's Best Restaurant. Its menus grow out of around five hectares of terraced gardens farmed in biodynamic ways.
new.tip: Reservations open months ahead in monthly batches, so set a reminder.
new.q: Mirazur, 30 Avenue Aristide Briand, Menton

new.title: Lunch among the artists at Les Arcades in Biot
new.desc: In 1952 André Brothier opened a shop under the arcades of Biot's main square. Fernand Léger rented a room from him, Chagall and Picasso came by, and Mimi's cooking turned it into a restaurant hung with art. His family still runs it.
new.tip: Order the Provençal classics, such as stuffed courgette flowers or rabbit, and look at the art on the walls.
new.q: Les Arcades, 16 Place des Arcades, Biot

new.title: Watch the jam pans at Maison Herbin in Menton
new.desc: A family jam maker in Menton's old town since the 1970s, cooking small batches in copper pans. The Menton lemon is the star, in marmalades and lemon spreads.
new.tip: Free workshop visits run on Monday, Wednesday and Friday mornings at 10. Book ahead.
new.q: Maison Herbin, 2 Rue Palmaro, Menton

new.title: Drink rum from a coconut at Pam Pam
new.desc: A lively Brazilian themed bar in Juan-les-Pins, popular since the 1920s, famous for its tropical cocktails and ice cream sundaes. In summer there are dance shows every night.
new.tip: It gets busy late in July and August, so come early in the evening for a table.
new.q: Pam Pam, Boulevard du Président Wilson, Juan-les-Pins

new.title: Toast the Jazz Age at the Bar Fitzgerald
new.desc: The Hôtel Belles Rives in Juan-les-Pins was once the Villa Saint-Louis, rented by F. Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald in 1926. The same family has run the hotel since 1929, and its piano bar carries the writer's name.
new.tip: Order a cocktail at sunset over the bay. The hotel closes in winter.
new.q: Hôtel Belles Rives, 33 Boulevard Édouard Baudoin, Juan-les-Pins

new.title: Order a seafood platter at Astoux et Brun
new.desc: A Cannes institution since 1953, run by the same family for three generations. Oysters, shellfish and crustaceans are piled high on platters just behind the old port.
new.tip: Seafood is served all day, which makes it a good late lunch after the Lérins boats.
new.q: Astoux et Brun, 27 Rue Félix Faure, Cannes

new.title: Join the flower battle at the Fête des Violettes
new.desc: On the first weekend of March, Tourrettes-sur-Loup celebrates the violets grown on its terraces. Since 1952 the village has decorated its lanes with flowers, and a flower float parade ends in a flower battle on Place de la Libération.
new.tip: The parade is on Sunday afternoon. Park lower down and walk up, as the village gets packed.
new.q: Place de la Libération, Tourrettes-sur-Loup

new.title: Get sprayed with jasmine water at the Fête du Jasmin
new.desc: Every first weekend of August since 1946, Grasse celebrates the flower that made its perfume famous. Flower floats parade through town, and firefighters spray the crowd with jasmine scented water.
new.tip: The night parade on Saturday is the highlight. Wear clothes you do not mind getting wet.
new.q: Place aux Aires, Grasse

new.title: Hear jazz under the pines at Jazz à Juan
new.desc: Since 1960 the Pinède Gould in Juan-les-Pins has hosted one of Europe's oldest jazz festivals each July. Louis Armstrong, Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Ella Fitzgerald and Ray Charles all played under these pines.
new.tip: Book early for the big names, and arrive in time for a swim on the beach next to the pine grove.
new.q: Pinède Gould, Juan-les-Pins

new.title: Watch glassblowers at the Verrerie de Biot
new.desc: Founded in 1956 by Éloi Monod, the Verrerie de Biot invented bubble glass, trapping tiny bubbles between layers of glass. You can watch the glassblowers at work in their hall.
new.tip: Entry to the glassblowers' hall, shop and galleries is free. Paid guided tours run in summer.
new.q: Verrerie de Biot, Chemin des Combes, Biot

new.title: Watch wolves from the hides of Parc Alpha
new.desc: At 1,500 metres in the Boréon, above Saint-Martin-Vésubie and at the edge of the Mercantour national park, Parc Alpha lets you watch wolf packs from wooden hides in the forest.
new.tip: Dress warmly even in summer, and call ahead outside the summer season to check opening.
new.q: Parc Alpha, Le Boréon, Saint-Martin-Vésubie

new.title: Hear chamber music on the parvis at Menton
new.desc: Since its first concert in August 1950, the Festival de Musique de Menton has held summer evening concerts outdoors on the pebble mosaic square in front of the Basilique Saint-Michel, high above the sea.
new.tip: It runs from late July into August. Book ahead for the evening concerts, and arrive early to watch the sun set over the old town.
new.q: Parvis de la Basilique Saint-Michel-Archange, Menton

new.title: Ski within two hours of the beach at Isola 2000
new.desc: Built in 1971 at around 2,000 metres, Isola 2000 is about 90 kilometres from Nice yet offers some 120 kilometres of pistes. Niçois head up for a day on the snow and are back by the sea for dinner.
new.tip: Leave early on weekends to beat the traffic in the Tinée valley.
new.q: Isola 2000
